<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:CGH}
For every odd $n$, all irreducible factors of $F_n$ are monogenic.  For every even $n$, all
irreducible factors of $L_n$ are monogenic.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
In what follows, all roots are taken in a fixed algebraic closure $\overline\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{C}$.  For an integer
$n\ge1$ we write $\zeta_n:=e^{2\pi i/n}$, a primitive $n$-th root of unity,
$\varphi$ will stand for Euler's totient function, $\Phi_m(X)$ for the $m$-th cyclotomic polynomial, and
$\mathcal{O}_K$ for the ring of integers of a number field $K$. An element $\zeta$ is a {primitive $m$-th root of unity} if it has order exactly $m$ in
$\mathbb{C}^\times$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $k,s$ be nonzero integers and let $t=\pm s^2$.  Let $n\ge1$, and let $f$ be an irreducible factor of $F_n^{(k,t)}$ or
$L_n^{(k,t)}$. Let $x\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ be a root of $f$ and set $ \theta:=\frac{k\,x}{s}.$
Then $\theta$ is an algebraic integer, $\mathbb{Q}(\theta)=\mathbb{Q}(x)$, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(x)}=\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$.
 Moreover, there exists a root of unity $\xi$ such that $\theta$ has the form indicated in the last column of the following table. 
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\hline
$t$ & family & hypothesis on $n$ & $\theta$ equals\\
\hline
$+s^2$ & $F^{(k,t)}_n$ & $n$ odd & $\xi-\xi^{-1}$\\
$+s^2$ & $L^{(k,t)}_n$ & $n$ even, $n\ge2$ & $\xi-\xi^{-1}$\\
$-s^2$ & $F^{(k,t)}_n$ & $n\ge1$ & $\xi+\xi^{-1}$\\
$-s^2$ & $L^{(k,t)}_n$ & $n\ge1$ & $\xi+\xi^{-1}$\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:CGH}
For every odd $n$, all irreducible factors of $F_n$ are monogenic.  For every even $n$, all
irreducible factors of $L_n$ are monogenic.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:main}
Let $u:=\zeta+c\,\zeta^{-1}$. Suppose that $\mathbb{Q}(u)$ is a proper subfield of $K$, then $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)}=\mathbb{Z}[u]$.  In particular;
$\mathbb{Q}(u)$ is monogenic.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:shift}
Let $N\ge0$, and let $a_0,\dots,a_N\in\mathbb{Q}$. Define
$$ g(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k\,X^{\,N-k}\,(X^2+c)^{k}\ \in\mathbb{Q}[X].$$
Then, $\deg g\le 2N$, the coefficient of $X^{2N}$ in $g$ is $a_N$, and
\[
   g(\zeta)=\zeta^{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k\,u^{k},\qquad u=\zeta+c\zeta^{-1}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For each $0\le k\le N$, the $k$-th summand has degree at most $(N-k)+2k=N+k\le 2N$, with equality only for $k=N$.
Since the polynomial $X^2+c$ is monic, it follows that $\deg g\le2N$  and the leading coefficient of $X^{2N}$ is $a_N$. 
Next, since $\zeta u=\zeta^2+c$, we have $\zeta^{N-k}(\zeta^2+c)^k=\zeta^{N-k}\zeta^{k}u^{k}=\zeta^{N}u^{k}$.
Therefore,
\[
g(\zeta)
=\sum_{k=0}^Na_k\zeta^{N-k}(\zeta^2+c)^k
=\zeta^N\sum_{k=0}^Na_ku^k.
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:degree}
If $\mathbb{Q}(u)$ is a proper subfield of $K$, then
$2[\mathbb{Q}(u):\mathbb{Q}]\le\varphi(m).$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Write $d=[\mathbb{Q}(u):\mathbb{Q}]$. By the Tower Law,
 $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=[K:\mathbb{Q}(u)][\mathbb{Q}(u):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(m)$. Hence $d\mid\varphi(m)$. Since $\mathbb{Q}(u)\subsetneq K$, we have $d<\varphi(m)$, and hence $\varphi(m)/d\ge2$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
It is enough to prove that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}[u]$. Let
$d=[\mathbb{Q}(u):\mathbb{Q}]$.

We first prove the following claim.

\medskip

\noindent
{Claim.}
If $a_0,\ldots,a_N\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $2N<\varphi(m)$ and $\alpha=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_ku^k$
is an algebraic integer, then $a_0,\ldots,a_N\in\mathbb{Z}$.

\medskip

We prove by induction on $N$. The case $N=0$ is trivial. It suffices to prove that
$a_N\in\mathbb{Z}$, since $\alpha-a_Nu^N$ is again an algebraic integer of the same form. Let $g$ be the polynomial defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:shift}. Then
$g(\zeta)=\zeta^N\alpha,~
\deg g\le2N,$
and the leading coefficient of $g$ is $a_N$.
Since $\zeta^N\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$, there exists
$f\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ with $\deg f<\varphi(m)$ and
$f(\zeta)=\zeta^N\alpha$, after replacing $f$ by its remainder modulo $\Phi_m$, if necessary.
Hence $(g-f)(\zeta)=0.$
As $\deg(g-f)<\varphi(m)=\deg\Phi_m,$
we obtain $g=f$.  Hence
$a_N\in\mathbb{Z}$, proving the claim.


Now let $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(u)}$. Since
$\{1,u,\ldots,u^{d-1}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $\mathbb{Q}(u)$, we may write
\[
\alpha=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}a_ku^k,
\qquad a_k\in\mathbb{Q}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree}, $2(d-1)<\varphi(m).$
Hence the claim applies and yields $a_k\in\mathbb{Z}$ for every $0\le k\le d-1$. Thus
$\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[u]$, and the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:proper}
The field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta+c\zeta^{-1})$ is a proper subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ if and only if there exists a primitive $m$-th root of unity $\beta\ne\zeta$ such that $ \beta+c\beta^{-1}=\zeta+c\zeta^{-1}.$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Suppose that such $\beta$ exists.
Since $\beta$ and $\zeta$ are roots of $\Phi_m$, there exists
$\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ with $\sigma(\zeta)=\beta$. Hence
$\sigma(u)=u$. If $\mathbb{Q}(u)=K$, then $\sigma$ fixes a generator of $K$ and therefore
$\sigma=\mathrm{id}$, contradicting the fact that $\beta\ne\zeta$. 

Conversely, suppose that $\mathbb{Q}(u)\subsetneq K$. Since $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois, there exists a
nontrivial automorphism $\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ which fixes $\mathbb{Q}(u)$ pointwise. Putting
$\beta=\sigma(\zeta)$, we have $\beta\ne\zeta$, $\beta$ is again a primitive $m$-th root
of unity, and $\beta+c\beta^{-1}
=\sigma(\zeta+c\zeta^{-1})
=\sigma(u)
=u.$ This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:critA}
Let $N\ge1$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\alpha^{2N}=-1$ and $\alpha^2\neq-1$.  Then the field $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha-\alpha^{-1})$ is monogenic. Precisely,
$\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha-\alpha^{-1})}=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha-\alpha^{-1}]$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By hypothesis, we see that $\alpha$ is a root of unity. Let $m$ be its order. So,
$m\mid 4N$.  Set $\beta:=-\alpha^{-1}$.  Since $\alpha^{2N}=-1,$ we have
$\beta=\alpha^{2N-1}$.  Let $\gcd(2N-1,m)=e$. Then $e$ is odd. Hence
$\gcd(e,4)=1$ and $e\mid N$. This implies that $e$ divides both $2N$ and $2N-1$, and thus $e=1$.  Therefore,
$\beta$ is again a primitive $m$-th root of unity.  Moreover $\beta\neq\alpha$, 
because $\alpha^2\neq-1$ by hypothesis, and $\beta-\beta^{-1}=-\alpha^{-1}+\alpha$.  Keeping in mind Lemma~\ref{lem:proper}
with $c=-1$, we have $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha-\alpha^{-1})\neq\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. 
The proof is complete by Proposition~\ref{prop:main}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:washington}
For any integer $m>2$, the maximal real subfield
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})$ is monogenic, with
$\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})}
=
\mathbb{Z}[\zeta+\zeta^{-1}].$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Take $c=1$ and $\beta=\zeta^{-1}$. Since $m>2$, we have
$\beta\ne\zeta$, and
$\beta+\beta^{-1}=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}.$
Hence the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:proper} is satisfied, and the conclusion follows immediately from Proposition~\ref{prop:main}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:critB}
Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ be a root of unity with $\alpha^2\neq1$.  Then
$\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha+\alpha^{-1})}=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha+\alpha^{-1}]$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:nakahara}
If $m>4$ and $4$ divides $ m$, then the field
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta-\zeta^{-1})$ is monogenic with $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\zeta-\zeta^{-1})}
=
\mathbb{Z}[\zeta-\zeta^{-1}].$
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Take $c=-1$ and $\beta=-\zeta^{-1}$.  Since $4$ divides $ m$, we have $\zeta^{m/2}=-1$ and
$\beta=\zeta^{m/2-1}$. Keeping in mind the fact that $\frac{m}{2}-1$ is odd, it is easy to see that $\gcd\!\left(\frac{m}{2}-1,m\right)=1.$ Thus
$\beta$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity. Also,
$\beta-\beta^{-1}=-\zeta^{-1}+\zeta$, and $\beta\neq\zeta$. So the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:proper} is satisfied. Now, applying Proposition~\ref{prop:main}, we are done.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Let $n>1$ be odd and let $\alpha=i\zeta_n$. Then $\alpha$ is a primitive
$4n$-th root of unity and
$\alpha-\alpha^{-1}
=
-i(\zeta_{2n}+\zeta_{2n}^{-1}).$
Using Corollary~\ref{cor:nakahara}, we get
\cite[Proposition~4.1]{CGH}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:dickson}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $a\in R$.  The {Dickson polynomials of the first and
second kind with parameter $a$} to be denoted by $D^{(1)}_n(X;a),\,D^{(2)}_n(X;a)\in R[X]$ are the sequences defined recursively by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dickson}
\begin{aligned}
  D^{(1)}_0(X;a)&=2, & D^{(1)}_1(X;a)&=X, &
  D^{(1)}_{n+2}(X;a)&=X\,D^{(1)}_{n+1}(X;a)-a\,D^{(1)}_{n}(X;a),\\
  D^{(2)}_0(X;a)&=1, & D^{(2)}_1(X;a)&=X, &
  D^{(2)}_{n+2}(X;a)&=X\,D^{(2)}_{n+1}(X;a)-a\,D^{(2)}_{n}(X;a).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For any $x\in R$ we will write $D^{(j)}_n(x;a)\in R$ for the value of this polynomial at $x$, and we
abbreviate $D^{(j)}_n$ when $a$ is clear from the context.  Note that both are monic of degree $n$ for $n\ge1$ (see \cite{LMT}).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:kt-is-dickson}
For $n\ge0$ and $k,t\in\mathbb Z$,
$$ F^{(k,t)}_{n+1}(X)=D^{(2)}_n(kX;-t),\qquad L^{(k,t)}_{n}(X)=D^{(1)}_n(kX;-t).$$
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:binet}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $x,\alpha,\beta,a $ belonging to $R$ satisfies $\alpha+\beta=x$ and
$\alpha\beta=a$.  Then for every $n\ge0$, 
\[
   D^{(1)}_n(x;a)=\alpha^n+\beta^n,\qquad
   (\alpha-\beta)\,D^{(2)}_n(x;a)=\alpha^{n+1}-\beta^{n+1}.
\]
If $\alpha=\beta$, so that $x=2\alpha$ and $a=\alpha^2$, then
\[
   D^{(1)}_n(x;a)=2\alpha^{n},\qquad
   \alpha\,D^{(2)}_n(x;a)=(n+1)\,\alpha^{n+1}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Keeping in mind the defining recurrence of the Dickson polynomials and the
hypothesis, the proof follows by induction on $n$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:rescale}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $a,c\in R$. Then, for every $n\ge0$ and
$j\in\{1,2\}$, $ D^{(j)}_n\bigl(cX;\;c^2a\bigr)=c^{\,n}\,D^{(j)}_n(X;a).$
In particular, if $c$ is a unit in $R$ and $x$ is a root of
$D_n^{(j)}(X;c^2a)$, then $x/c$ is a root of $D_n^{(j)}(X;a)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The result follows by induction on $n$ and the final assertion follows by evaluating the identity at $X=x/c$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Fix $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{C}$.  The {characteristic polynomial} of the recurrence
\eqref{eq:dickson} at the point $x$ is given by
\[
   \chi_{x,a}(Y):=Y^2-xY+a\ \in\mathbb{C}[Y].
\]
 Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}$ be its two roots. Then, the relations
 $\alpha+\beta=x,\qquad \alpha\beta=a,$
 tpgether with Lemma~\ref{lem:binet} gives the corresponding Dickson polynomials
 in terms of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:nondeg} Let $a\ne0$ and let $x$ be a root of either
 $D_m^{(1)}(\,\cdot\,;a)$ or  $D_m^{(2)}(\,\cdot\,;a)$. Then the roots
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ of $\chi_{x,a}$ are distinct.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $\alpha\beta=a\ne0$, we have $\alpha\ne0$. If $\alpha=\beta$, Lemma~\ref{lem:binet}
gives $(m+1)\alpha^{m+1}=0$ or $2\alpha^m=0$, which is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:alpha}
Let $a\neq0$. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{it:fst} If $D^{(1)}_m(x;a)=0$, then $\alpha^{2m}=-a^{m}$.
\item\label{it:sec} If $D^{(2)}_m(x;a)=0$, then $\alpha^{2(m+1)}=a^{m+1}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Using Lemmas~\ref{lem:nondeg} and~\ref{lem:binet}, respectively, we have $\alpha\neq\beta$,~
$\alpha^m=-\beta^m$ and $\alpha^{m+1}=\beta^{m+1}$. Keeping in mind the relation, 
$\alpha\beta=a$, the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:kt-is-dickson}, $x$ is a root of $F^{(k,t)}_{n}$ if and only if $kx$ is a
root of $D^{(2)}_{n-1}(\,\cdot\,;-t)$, and a root of $L^{(k,t)}_{n}$ if and only if $kx$ is a
root of $D^{(1)}_{n}(\,\cdot\,;-t)$. Keeping in mind Lemma~\ref{lem:rescale}, 
without loss of generality, we may assume that $k=s=1$, so  $a:=-t=\pm1$ and it
is enough to prove $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(x)}=\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
 
 Let $\beta=x-\alpha$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:nondeg}, we have $\alpha\ne\beta$, and
 $\alpha\ne0$ since $\alpha\beta=a\ne0$. Now, we split the proof into two cases.

\noindent {Case 1: When $a=-1$, i.e., $t=1$.}  Here $\alpha\beta=-1$, so $\beta=-\alpha^{-1}$ and
$x=\alpha+\beta=\alpha-\alpha^{-1}$. Moreover,
$\alpha^2\neq-1$.  Suppose that $x$ is a root of $D_{n-1}^{(2)}$ with $n$ odd, or of $D_n^{(1)}$ with $n$ even. Then using Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha}, it is easy to see that $\alpha^{2n}=-1$. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:critA} with $N=n$, we have $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(x)}=\mathbb{Z}[x].$ Taking $\xi=\alpha$, we get $x=\xi-\xi^{-1}$.\\
\noindent {Case 2: When $a=1$ , i.e.,  $t=-1$.}   Here $\alpha\beta=1$, and hence
$x=\alpha+\alpha^{-1}$ and $\alpha^2\ne1$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha}, we see that
$\alpha^{2n}=1$ or $-1$, according as $x$ is a root of
$D_{n-1}^{(2)}$ or $D_n^{(1)}$. So, $\alpha$ is a root of unity, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(x)}=\mathbb{Z}[x]$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:critB}. Taking
$\xi=\alpha$ yields $x=\xi+\xi^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Take $k=s=t=1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Then $\theta=x$, and the
result follows immediately.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:cheb}
The {Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind} are defined by
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n$$ and
  $$U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n  $$ respectively.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:cheb}
For any $n\ge1$, the following assertions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every irreducible factor of $S_n$ or $C_n$ is monogenic;
\item If $x$ is a root of $U_n$ or $T_n$, then
$\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(x)}=\mathbb{Z}[2x].$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The first assertion follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:main} by taking $k=1$, $t=-1$,
and the second by taking $k=2,~t=-1$ together with the fact that
$U_n(X)=S_n(2X)$ and $2T_n(X)=C_n(2X)$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
